title: Contracts, scripts, data & docs — everything that isn't application code

overview.l1: This is the project's paper trail and its data supply chain — everything that is not Rust server code or C# client code, but that both depend on. Open datasets (KJV text, geocoding, Theographic metadata, catechism and commentary corpora) land in data/raw/, get hand-curated and corrected in data/curated/ (TOML files a human can read and edit), then two build-time programs compile all of that into data/compiled/ — most importantly graph.bin, the one file the server loads at startup. data/exports/ hands three smaller files to a sibling map project. Around all of that sits a pre-push gate (scripts/) built from a vendored contract-testing engine (contracts/) that refuses to let code and its promises to other systems drift apart. docs/ records the design decisions and plans that got the project here, and README.md/LICENSES.md are the front door and the paper trail for every source used.
overview.l2: The data flow is a pipeline with two compile steps. Step one, `atlas-etl`, reads data/raw/ (fetched by data/fetch-raw.ps1, gitignored) plus data/curated/ (committed TOML, hand-authored) and writes most of data/compiled/*.json plus report.txt — a validation report that fails the build loud on bad references. Step two, `atlas-graph-compile`, reads the same raw+curated inputs and writes data/compiled/graph.bin, the single serialized 'Explorable Graph' every server query answers from, plus the three files in data/exports/ for the map project, all in one pass so they can never drift apart. The server (`atlas-server`) loads graph.bin and the surviving *.json sidecars at startup; the client only ever sees HTTP JSON. Wrapped around this data pipeline is a second system: contracts/ holds Gherkin (plain-English behavioral test) suites that state what other systems — and the client — may rely on, executed by a vendored Haskell test runner (contracts/runner/); scripts/contract-gate.sh runs before every `git push` and refuses to push if any contract's promise and the real code disagree. docs/superpowers/ is the paper trail: specs/ record design decisions (the graph model, the frontend/backend contract, the SQLite migration plan), plans/ record how a batch of work was actually executed.
overview.l3: Concretely: `data/raw/README.md` documents the exact JSON/JSONL/HTML shapes of every fetched dataset (verified against real files, not assumed from a spec); `data/fetch-raw.ps1` is the idempotent fetch script, pinning several sources to commit SHAs for reproducibility. `data/curated/*.toml` (~22 top-level files plus narratives/, passages/, polities/ subfolders) are hand-authored corrections, additions and organizational data no open dataset provides — narratives, eras, polity borders, catechism text, chronology anchors — each parsed by a dedicated function in `server/atlas-etl/src/curated.rs` and validated in `server/atlas-etl/src/validate.rs`. `data/compiled/` holds the ETL's JSON outputs (loaded by `server/atlas-core/src/data.rs`) plus `graph.bin` (bincode-serialized, loaded by `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs` and `service.rs`) plus `report.txt` (coverage stats). `data/exports/` carries three JSON files stamped with `atlas_version_root`, written by `server/atlas-graph/src/exports.rs` in the same pass as graph.bin so they can never disagree with it. The contract layer: `contracts/SUITES` is the registry mapping each contract directory to the harness that owns it; `contracts/atlas-graph-contract` and `contracts/atlas-query-contract` are the atlas's own promises (about its graph, and about its query language, respectively — deliberately non-overlapping); `contracts/atlas-edge` and `contracts/map-api-consumer` are RECEIVED and SENT cross-repo promises with the sibling map-generator project; `contracts/pacts` are recorded request/response fixtures used to run the suites offline; `contracts/runner` is a vendored (not reimplemented) Haskell Gherkin executor. `scripts/contract-gate.sh` derives its inventory of what must pass entirely from committed git content (never the working tree) specifically because three rounds of adversarial review found ways to disarm a gate that trusted any deletable marker file.

files.role: Front door: what the app is, how to install, run, test, and regenerate data.
files.l1: README.md is the first thing anyone reads: what Bible Explorer does (a KJV reader, a `/world` map with a time slider, catechism and commentary links), what to install, and the exact commands to run the server and client side by side. It also states the single most important fact about the whole repo: everything under `data/` is machine-generated from open datasets by two build-time programs — nobody hand-types the graph. If this file vanished, a newcomer would have no way to know that `data/compiled/` is already committed and ready to run with zero setup, or which two commands to run after editing the curated data.
files.l2: The file walks top to bottom through the project lifecycle: Prerequisites (Rust stable, a one-time Windows `dlltool` workaround via `server/setup-toolchain.ps1`, .NET 10, Node 24), Data (explains that `data/compiled/graph.bin` is the one artifact every feature queries, generated by `atlas-graph-compile`, while a handful of separate `data/compiled/*.json` files are generated by `atlas-etl` and not yet folded into the graph), the exact two-binary regeneration recipe (`cargo run -p atlas-etl` then `cargo run -p atlas-graph --release --bin atlas-graph-compile`), the Dev loop (two terminals: the Rust API on port 8000, the Blazor dev server on port 5000, connected by permissive CORS since there's no dev proxy), Tests (a two-command Rust count plus xunit plus a Playwright property suite, with a documented 'deep exhaustive run' two-tier mode for stress-testing), the Publish path (one self-contained `atlas-server` binary serving both API and client, same-origin), and Licenses (a summary table, pointing at LICENSES.md for the full record). It's prose and shell/PowerShell snippets, not code — there's nothing to compile here, only commands to copy.
files.l3: Load-bearing details a returning contributor would want: the windows-gnu toolchain's bundled `dlltool` needs a GNU assembler this machine doesn't have, so `server/setup-toolchain.ps1` provisions a renamed `llvm-ar.exe` as a substitute, and `server/.cargo/config.toml` points `rustflags` at that literal, user-specific path. `atlas-etl` and `atlas-graph-compile` are two SEPARATE binaries, not one pipeline — `atlas-graph-compile` runs its own artifact through two independent ADMISSION passes before writing anything, which is why it takes 'tens of seconds' even though it reads the same inputs as `atlas-etl`. Regeneration overwrites the committed `data/compiled/`, and `graph.bin`'s own byte-determinism is a committed test (`server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs`) — an unexpected diff there is a real bug, not noise. The test-count law: `cargo test --workspace` cannot reach `atlas-graph-types` (a real sibling crate outside the default workspace membership per `server/Cargo.toml`'s own 'STANDING COUNTING PROCEDURE' comment), so the canonical total is the SUM of two separate commands (828 = 806 + 22) — a newcomer running only the first command would under-count. Explicitly calls out never running `dotnet build`/`dotnet test` on `client` while its dev server is live (corrupts the served WASM, 'a proven flake source'), and never touching a port other than 8000/5000 that isn't yours (the system's own git-status context corroborates this: port 8080 is reserved for something else entirely). The publish path's SPA fallback returns a real HTTP 200 for deep links, not tower-http's native 404, pinned by a named test in `server/atlas-server/tests/api.rs`.

files.role: The canonical, per-source license and provenance record for every dataset used.
files.l1: LICENSES.md is the paper trail proving every piece of text and data in this app is legally usable — the King James Bible, Luther's Small Catechism, historical map borders, even the tile images the map shows live. For each source it says exactly what license applies, how the source is used (baked into the app, or only ever fetched live and never stored), and — for anything with a real editorial judgment call behind it — walks through how the project verified the source is what it claims to be. If this file vanished, nobody could tell whether the app is safe to publish.
files.l2: Opens with a per-source table (one row per dataset: KJV text, OpenBible geocoding, Theographic metadata, map tile services, Luther's Small Catechism, the Book of Concord, Kretzmann's commentary, and more), then has one long narrative section per source that needed real investigative work: sourcing, two-independent-copy verification (quoting exact matched passages), what was actually used versus merely consulted, and a 'dedication' paragraph distinguishing the source's own public-domain text from this project's own organizational work (dedicated CC0). It ends with a per-compiled-artifact label table and a catch-all 'everything not listed here' rule. It's Markdown prose with embedded links and quoted verbatim text — no code, but written with the same rigor a legal filing would need.
files.l3: The structural pattern repeated across ~10 sections (Small Catechism, Book of Concord, catechism verse mapping, Robertson's Harmony, Crockett's Harmony, Ussher's Annals, Easton's Dictionary, brain-fuel/bible editions, Kretzmann's commentary, KJV red-letter markup) is always Source/Verification/What-was-used/Dedication — each makes an explicit, checkable claim (e.g. 'the First Commandment's explanation reads verbatim...', cross-checked against a second independent source word-for-word) rather than an assertion taken on faith. Notable rulings: the Theographic dataset is CC BY-SA 4.0 (share-alike) and the project's controller explicitly ruled this does NOT block public release, since dropping it would cost 81.5% of dated events; historical polity borders were originally a GPL-3.0 dataset and were entirely replaced with this project's own hand-drawn, CC0 coordinates (documented down to which specific Wikipedia pages were read for which polity, and which eras were drawn from unverified general knowledge, disclosed as such). The KJV red-letter markup section explains why a GPL-licensed CrossWire module was rejected in favor of an alternate public-domain OSIS source with the identical `<q who="Jesus">` convention. Every 'what was used' paragraph is careful to separate the SOURCE's own words (quoted, license-bound) from this project's own phrasing of displayed titles (always CC0, never the secondary source's archaic wording).

files.role: The original Haskell type-level sketch the whole project's design grew from.
files.l1: This is the very first draft of the idea, written in Haskell before a line of Rust or C# existed. It sketches, as types rather than working code, the shapes the project still uses today: a place with a location, a time range, a Bible verse belonging to a passage belonging to a chapter belonging to a book, and — the key idea — an "Explorable" thing: anything you're looking at can hand you a list of related things to look at next. The file still sits untouched at the repo root as the conceptual blueprint everything else was built to realize.
files.l2: It defines newtypes for `Latitude`/`Longitude`, a `Location`, a `TimeRange`, and a `TimeAndPlace` pair; a `BibleRef` closed union (Book/Chapter/Passage/Verse, each wrapping a `Set` of the level below); typeclasses (`TimeAndPlaceQuery`, `BibleRefQuery`) that let one function work for several different query-key types (an 'overloaded lookup' idiom — Rust's closest analogue is a trait implemented for several concrete types). The centerpiece is `class Explorable e where explore :: e a -> (a -> [e b]) -> [e b]` — deliberately monad-shaped (bind), and `SomeExplorable` is an existential wrapper (`ExistentialQuantification`) letting a list hold different `Explorable` types together, the same problem C#'s `IExplorable` interface later solves by ordinary interface erasure. Several functions (`getTimeRange`, `getBibleTimeAndPlace`) are left as `undefined` — genuinely unimplemented placeholders, since this file was never meant to run, only to declare shapes.
files.l3: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-22-explorable-graph-types.md` §0 explicitly supersedes this file's own `explore` signature: using `[e b]` (a list) instead of a genuine `Set` was 'an encoding workaround for an Ord constraint... and is SUPERSEDED: it put multiplicity outside e and broke the monad shape' — the real design moved multiplicity INSIDE a proper `Explore` monad (`newtype Explore a = Explore (Set (Position, a))`). `Discovery { discoveryFocus, discoveryCrossRefs, discoveryTimeAndPlace }` survives conceptually as 'the VIEW — the screen shape for one position' in the current design. The file needs three GHC language extensions (`ExistentialQuantification`, `FlexibleInstances`, `TypeSynonymInstances`) purely to let `Author` (a `type` synonym for `String`) be used as a typeclass instance head — a Haskell wrinkle with no Rust equivalent (Rust's trait system has no analogous 'flexible instance' restriction to work around). This file is never compiled or tested by anything else in the repo; it is read-only documentation of intent, cited by `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-17-bible-atlas-design.md`'s own line 5 as 'the type-level sketch this design realizes.'

files.role: What the repo excludes from version control, with reasoning for each exception.
files.l1: This file tells git which files and folders never to track: build output (Rust's `target/`, .NET's `bin`/`obj`), Node's `node_modules`, and — deliberately NOT excluded — `data/compiled/`, which is committed on purpose so a fresh clone runs immediately with no download step. It's short but each line carries a reason in a comment, because getting this file wrong either bloats the repo with junk or accidentally hides something the app needs to run.
files.l2: Structured in commented sections: GHC artifacts from the Haskell sketch (`*.hi`/`*.o`), Rust `target/`, .NET `bin`/`obj`, then a `data/raw/*` exclusion with an explicit `!data/raw/README.md` negation (everything in raw/ is gitignored except its own README, since raw data is refetchable but the README documenting its shape is not), Node/test tooling, and a comment explaining why `client/wwwroot/vendor/` (vendored Leaflet) is deliberately COMMITTED despite being third-party code — omitting it would make a fresh clone's `index.html` load the SPA fallback page instead of the Leaflet library, silently breaking the map with a cryptic "Unexpected token '<'" error.
files.l3: The `data/raw/*` plus `!data/raw/README.md` pairing is the key non-obvious pattern here: git's ignore-then-unignore ordering matters (a later `!` pattern can only re-include a path if none of its parent directories were themselves ignored, which is why `data/raw/*` — not `data/raw/` — is used). `publish/` is separately ignored at the bottom as `dotnet publish`'s own build output. This file is read only by git itself; nothing in the codebase parses or tests it, so a change here is invisible to CI other than by what subsequently shows up (or fails to show up) in `git status`.

files.role: The git pre-push hook that runs the contract gate before every push.
files.l1: This is a small script that, once a developer opts in with one `git config` command, git runs automatically every time they try to push — and if the contract gate (scripts/contract-gate.sh) fails, the push is refused outright. It exists because the owner wanted a hard technical guarantee, not a policy reminder, that code and its promises to other systems can never silently drift apart. It reads which specific commits are about to be pushed (not just whatever HEAD happens to be) so the check is always about what's actually being sent, and there is deliberately no way to skip it short of git's own `--no-verify` escape hatch, which leaves a visible trace.
files.l2: Bash script installed via `.git/hooks` by running `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` — tracked here (unlike the default `.git/hooks` location) so the hook itself is reviewed and versioned like any other file, even though arming it is still a local, per-clone decision. It reads git's own pre-push stdin protocol (`<local ref> <local sha> <remote ref> <remote sha>` per line) to find the REMOTE side's current commit, which becomes the base the semver gate diffs against — the correct base, since it's exactly what the receiving repository will see change. Falls back to the gate's own resolution chain if no usable remote sha is found (e.g. pushing a brand-new branch). Guards on `[ -t 0 ]` so running the file directly from a terminal (how it's normally reviewed) doesn't hang waiting for piped input.
files.l3: Comment block documents its own history: it used to always gate `HEAD` against `@{upstream}` regardless of what was actually being pushed, a real scope gap labeled 'L-R2-4' fixed by reading git's own stdin protocol instead. Deliberately has no CI workflow alongside it, disclosed honestly as an open item rather than papered over with a workflow that couldn't run (the gate needs GHC, cabal, the Rust toolchain, and the committed graph artifact — none of which a bare GitHub Actions runner has by default). Calls `bash scripts/contract-gate.sh` (optionally with `--base "$REMOTE_BASE"`), checks its exit code, and prints a pointed remediation message on failure naming the exact remedy (bump the affected suite's VERSION + CHANGELOG). No test file directly exercises this hook; `scripts/gate-selftest.sh` tests the gate it calls, not this wrapper.

files.role: One-time Windows setup: provisions a working dlltool for the Rust GNU toolchain.
files.l1: On this machine's Rust toolchain, a step of the normal build process needs a small helper tool (`dlltool`) that isn't available in a form that works here. This script fixes that once per machine by copying and renaming an existing Rust tool (`llvm-ar.exe`) so it works as a stand-in. Run it before your first `cargo build`; after that it's a no-op every time (it checks whether the fix is already in place and exits immediately if so).
files.l2: PowerShell script: ensures `rustup component add llvm-tools` is installed (falling back to the older `llvm-tools-preview` name), locates `llvm-ar.exe` under the toolchain's sysroot for the `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` target, copies it to `~/.cargo/atlas-tools/llvm-dlltool.exe`, and — crucially — VERIFIES the renamed copy actually behaves as `dlltool` (checks its `--help` output mentions 'llvm-dlltool') before declaring success, deleting the bad copy if the check fails rather than leaving a broken binary in place. `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` makes any unhandled error fatal rather than silently continuing.
files.l3: The underlying problem, per its own comment and `server/.cargo/config.toml`: the `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` target's bundled GNU `dlltool` shells out to `as` (the GNU assembler) to build import libraries for `raw-dylib` (needed by `windows-sys >= 0.60`), and this machine has no `as`/C compiler by design. LLVM ships `ar`/`dlltool`/`nm` as one multicall binary that dispatches based on its own program name — so a byte-identical copy of `llvm-ar.exe`, simply renamed, runs as `dlltool` with zero additional download. The script is idempotent by construction (`if (Test-Path $dlltool) { exit 0 }`), and its own header notes the resulting path is embedded LITERALLY (not as an env-var expansion) in `server/.cargo/config.toml`'s `rustflags`, because cargo's config format doesn't expand environment variables there — so a different Windows username requires manually editing that config file to match.

files.role: The standing, evidence-based performance record for the server's query and startup paths.
files.l1: This file is where every performance claim about the server has to earn its place with a real measured number, not a guess. It records how fast the API answers different kinds of requests, how long the server takes to start up, how big the compiled data file is getting, and what was tried (including things that DIDN'T work) to make things faster. If a future change makes something slower, this file is the baseline that proves it.
files.l2: Organized around two batches (PERF-2a: the query surface and a suspected slow timeline slider; PERF-2b: startup/artifact-load time). Tables report criterion-benchmark medians for pure computation, real HTTP handlers, and generic graph endpoints, each annotated with WHY a number is what it is (e.g., "cost tracks how much of the graph is active, not window width in years"). A 'what was tried and rejected' section documents a memoization idea that measured no real improvement and was reverted, contrasted with the parallelization fix that WAS kept (with its exact percentage win). Ends with a size-growth table tracking `graph.bin`'s size against GitHub's 100MB file-size hard limit, flagging the remaining headroom as urgent.
files.l3: Concrete numbers worth knowing: `graph.bin` compiled artifact is 100,785,455 bytes with only ~3.88MB of headroom before GitHub's 104,857,600-byte hard block — the file directly documents which future corpus onboarding batch is most likely to hit that wall and what the three disclosed mitigation options are (git-lfs, splitting the artifact, or format-level compression), explicitly deferred to controller/owner decision. `Graph::build_indexes` was parallelized via `std::thread::scope`, achieving ~2.6x on that phase alone (from ~965-1030ms to ~365-375ms) by chunking both the node pool and edge pool off `std::thread::available_parallelism()` rather than a flat row-count constant — correctness was proven three separate ways: a dedicated unit test comparing chunked-then-merged output against the sequential algorithm, the full existing test suite passing unchanged, and a direct byte-for-byte HTTP response diff across five endpoints before/after the change. Discloses a real, reproducible flakiness in one LEGACY test's own artifact-load timing (not the real committed `graph.bin`'s own load path, which showed zero flaking across 10 runs) and documents the exact root-cause hypothesis (OS-level file I/O variance on a freshly-written temp file) without having chased it down, since it was out of that batch's scope.

files.role: Documents the real, verified shape of every fetched raw dataset, field by field.
files.l1: Before atlas-etl can read a downloaded dataset, someone has to know exactly what shape that file is really in — not what a spec assumed, but what it actually looks like when you open it. This file is that record: for every raw file the project downloads (the Bible text, place coordinates, historical event metadata, cross-references, and several more), it documents the real JSON/JSONL/HTML structure, field by field, including surprises found only by actually opening the files (a URL that moved, a field that turned out to be nested differently than expected, a value that's a string instead of a number).
files.l2: One section per source (KJV, OpenBible geocoding, Theographic metadata, cross-references, several vendored corpora added over time like the Book of Concord and Kretzmann's commentary, plus the Leaflet map library). Each section gives real sample JSON, calls out gotchas discovered only by reading the actual data (e.g. a nested stats object where a plain integer was expected; a resolution entry that can be a 'dead-end marker' with neither of two supposedly-required fields present), and states which fields atlas-etl's parser actually reads versus what's fetched but unused. files.role: Idempotent PowerShell script that downloads every raw dataset into data/raw/.
files.l1: This script fetches every external dataset the app needs — the Bible text, geocoding data, historical metadata, several public-domain classic texts — from the internet into `data/raw/`. It only downloads a file if it isn't already there, so running it again after a fresh clone or an interrupted run just fills in whatever's missing, never re-downloading what's already present. A handful of sources are pinned to a specific commit (not just "the latest version") so the same run always produces the same bytes.
files.l2: A single `Fetch($url, $out)` helper wraps `Invoke-WebRequest` with a `Test-Path` guard for idempotency. Sections handle each source in turn: KJV JSON, five OpenBible geocoding JSONL files, a Theographic metadata zip, a cross-references zip, several GitHub-commit-archive zips pinned by SHA (the user's own catechism mapping repo, six parallel-language Bible editions), ten Book-of-Concord HTML document pages plus 23 Smalcald Articles sub-pages fetched individually, 1,189 Kretzmann commentary chapter pages fetched with retry logic and a rate-limiting `Start-Sleep`, one large KJV red-letter OSIS XML file, and finally vendoring the Leaflet JS/CSS library into the client's `wwwroot`. Extensive inline comments record WHY each source is fetched the way it is (URL changes, license reasoning, controller decisions) rather than just what to fetch.
files.l3: Notably resilient in one place and simple everywhere else: the Kretzmann fetch loop (1,189 pages) retries each URL up to 3 times with linear backoff and explicitly disclaims falling back to any unverified URL scheme when the primary source fails — a genuine miss is logged and counted, never silently guessed at. The brain-fuel/bible fetch is SELECTIVE, not a whole-repo vendor: it extracts a ~29k-file upstream repo to a temp directory and copies out only the ~1,190 files this project's own parser actually reads (`data/books.json` plus every OT/NT chapter JSON), deleting the temp extraction and the source zip afterward — disclosed as an owner ruling ('no apocrypha for now') rather than a technical necessity. Historical border data is explicitly NOT fetched here anymore; a comment documents that a GPL-3.0 dataset that used to be fetched at this point in the script was removed entirely during a license remediation batch and replaced with hand-curated CC0 data living in `data/curated/polities/`.

files.role: The one serialized Explorable Graph artifact — the entire app's runtime truth.
files.l1: This is the single most important file the server reads: one big binary file holding the ENTIRE graph — every Bible verse, every cross-reference, every place, event, narrative, era, kingdom border, catechism link, Book of Concord paragraph, and commentary note — all as typed, connected records. If this file vanished, the server would have nothing to serve; regenerating it from scratch takes tens of seconds and re-derives everything from the raw and curated data. It's a binary file, not something a human opens directly — its size (over 100 MB) is tracked closely because GitHub refuses files over 100 MB.
files.l2: Produced by the `atlas-graph-compile` binary, which reads `data/raw/` + `data/curated/` and writes one `bincode`-serialized artifact using Rust's `serde` derive machinery. It carries a `FORMAT_VERSION` field so an old artifact from an incompatible schema is refused rather than silently misread. At load time (`server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs`, `service.rs`) the raw bytes are decoded, converted from wire DTOs into the in-memory domain types (`to_service_parts`), and then `Graph::build_indexes` builds every relation's bidirectional lookup index — a content-address hash (`pid`) per node and per edge occurrence, so any node or edge can be found by its id in O(1). This indexing step used to be the majority of server startup time and was parallelized with `std::thread::scope` to cut it by roughly half (documented in `server/BENCHMARKS.md`).
files.l3: Compiled by `server/atlas-graph/src/bins/compile_graph.rs`, which — per its own module doc comment — is deliberately kept SEPARATE from `atlas-etl` and runs the resulting artifact through TWO independent ADMISSION passes (`atlas_graph_types::store::assert_answers_match`, comparing the artifact-loaded graph against an independently-rebuilt from-source model) before writing anything to disk, a committed law, not a hope. Its own byte-determinism is pinned by `server/atlas-graph/tests/determinism.rs` — an unexpected diff on an unrelated change is itself a bug worth investigating. Identity today rests on Rust's `DefaultHasher` (unspecified algorithm, may change between Rust releases) over debug-print byte encoding — both flagged as real defects in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-relational-artifact-design.md` §3, which proposes replacing this whole file with a manifest-plus-SQLite-sections design specifically to fix identity and enable memory-mapped, page-level-resident loading instead of loading the entire ~100MB artifact into RAM at every startup. At 100,785,455 bytes, it sits within ~3.88MB of GitHub's 104,857,600-byte hard file-size limit — `BENCHMARKS.md` tracks exactly how much headroom remains after each corpus-adding batch and names git-lfs, artifact-splitting, and compression as disclosed, undecided mitigation options. Loaded once at server startup by `server/atlas-server/src/load.rs`/`main.rs`; never written to at runtime.

files.role: The pre-push contract gate: refuses to push when contracts and code disagree.
files.l1: This script is what actually runs when you try to `git push`, and it can refuse the push outright. Instead of just checking a short list of things that might be wrong, it works backwards from git's own committed history: it figures out the COMPLETE list of every promise this repo currently makes (every scenario in every contract suite), demands proof that every single one of them actually ran and passed, and refuses to pass if even one promise went unchecked. This inside-out design exists because three earlier, more ordinary versions of this script were each defeated by a different trick for making a broken promise look fine — deleting a marker file, renaming a suite's files away, or quietly re-labeling which test engine owns a suite. Under this version, none of those tricks removes anything the gate is checking; they only create a gap between what should have run and what did, and a gap is exactly what makes the gate fail.
files.l2: A bash script with eight numbered "legs," each independently checkable in its own printed section: leg 8 refuses any symlink or git submodule committed under `contracts/` (a way to make what the gate reads differ from what a checkout actually gets); leg 7 refuses to run at all if the working tree differs from the last commit on any path the gate grades (contracts/, data/exports/, server/, graph-types/) — a pre-push gate must grade what will actually be PUSHED, not what's sitting uncommitted on disk; leg 0 refuses to let a RECEIVED suite (another project's expectations of this one) be silently disarmed; legs 1 and 2 check every suite's totality and vocabulary; leg 3 rebuilds the recorded pact fixtures from the live graph and fails if they've drifted ("provider drift" — our own answers changed); leg 4 actually runs every scenario; leg 6 is the namesake inversion — it demands that every scenario the inventory says exists shows up in the results with a passing verdict, using MULTISET comparison (not set) so that two scenarios sharing a name can't hide one being silently deleted; leg 5 hands off to `contract-semver-gate.sh` to check that any suite whose contract changed bumped its version by the right amount. It resolves its own tools (`cargo`, `cabal`) from a small hard-coded list of absolute paths rather than trusting `$PATH` or an environment variable, specifically so a substituted or shadowed tool on `$PATH` can't quietly answer in the real tool's place.
files.l3: The script's own extensive header comments are a genuine incident report: they name three specific bypasses a security-style review found and closed in successive rounds — deleting `RECEIVED.md` (fixed by reading the received-suite list from git's committed HEAD, not the working tree); a one-word registry edit weakening a suite's declared harness (fixed by `contract-semver-gate.sh`'s harness ratchet, a row may only ever get STRONGER between two commits); and renaming a received suite's `.feature` files away, which an earlier version's own printed remedy (`ATLAS_BLESS_PACT=1 ...`) would have silently shrunk the evidence pact by 80% and turned the gate green. The trusted computing base is stated explicitly and narrowly (lines ~47-90): git itself, the POSIX shell toolchain, `cargo`/`cabal` at fixed compiled-in paths, and `contract-runner` (BUILT by this same script from source under version control, never looked up on PATH) — everything else (the working tree, any marker file's presence, `contracts/SUITES`'s own content, `python`, `sha256sum`) is explicitly NOT trusted and is either derived from committed git content or independently verified at runtime (e.g. the hashing tool used for leg 3's fingerprint is required to prove, by hashing two random byte strings on the spot, that it actually discriminates different inputs — closing a prior bypass where a hasher shim always printed the same constant). `--fast` skips only leg 3 (the slow recorder rebuild) and always exits 3, never 0, so it can never be mistaken for a full pass. Tested end-to-end, not just read, by `scripts/gate-selftest.sh`.

files.role: Classifies a contract's diff as PATCH/MINOR/MAJOR and refuses an under-declared version bump.
files.l1: When a contract file changes, this script figures out — by actually reading the diff, not by asking a human to self-report — whether that change is a small clarification (PATCH), an addition that doesn't break anyone (MINOR), or a real, breaking change to an existing promise (MAJOR), then refuses the push if the suite's own declared version bump is smaller than what the diff actually requires. Over-declaring is always fine; under-declaring is what this script exists to catch.
files.l2: Compares a suite's contract files at two git commits (never the working tree, on either side, per its own header's account of a real bug that comparing the working tree once caused) using the vendored `contract-runner grade` command for fixture value comparisons and its own `tags`/inventory subcommands for scenario-level comparison. Implements four one-way "ratchets": a suite's committed VERSION must be present and increasing; its declared harness in `contracts/SUITES` may only get STRONGER over time, never weaker; every scenario present at the base commit must still be present at HEAD; and a RECEIVED suite's marker file may never disappear once present. Any detected MAJOR change (a deleted/changed expectation, a re-blessed fixture with a different value, `@target` newly added to a previously-green scenario) requires a MAJOR version bump AND a CHANGELOG.md entry, or the gate refuses.
files.l3: The header's own account of three specific defects it once had, and their fixes, mirrors `contract-gate.sh`'s own incident-report style: comparing `git show base:file` against the raw WORKING TREE copy of the new file (rather than `HEAD:file`) meant a fixture re-blessed inside a commit but reverted only on disk graded as unchanged; the fixture-value comparison used to be answered by whatever `python` happened to be on PATH, gated by a three-constant calibration quiz that a nine-line shim satisfied; and the tag-parsing used to re-lex the vendored parser's own tab-separated output with a second `awk`, so a tab embedded INSIDE a scenario's own name could shift which column held `@target` and hide it from the classifier. All three are closed by routing every comparison through the same `contract-runner` binary the main gate builds, both git sides read via `git show`/`git cat-file`, and no output re-lexed a second time by shell tools. The `resolve_base` fallback chain deliberately excludes a bare `HEAD~1` fallback (removed because it silently classified a single unrelated commit as if it were the real base on a fresh clone where branch refs don't resolve) — an unresolvable base is now a hard failure with a clear message, never a quiet guess.

files.role: The gate's own test suite: every known way to lie to it, attempted for real and required to fail.
files.l1: This script doesn't just claim the contract gate is unbeatable — it actually TRIES to beat it, dozens of different ways (deleting files, renaming things, planting fake tools that pretend to do work, editing a registry to claim a weaker guarantee), and requires every single attempt to be refused. The philosophy stated in its own header: a comment claiming something is impossible is worth nothing; a test that tries the exploit and fails is worth exactly what it demonstrates.
files.l2: Two sections: section A runs real bypass attempts against the actual gate in the current worktree (every mutation restored afterward under a trap, verified with git), covering things like a fake `cargo`/`cabal` on PATH that answers correctly but does no real work, deleting a RECEIVED suite's marker, renaming a whole suite's feature files away, and every hashing tool on PATH printing a constant. Section B runs COMMITTED attacks inside disposable, throwaway git repositories (since the gate's ratchets are specifically about what's committed across two commits, which section A's uncommitted mutations can't exercise) — a scenario deleted with too small a declared version bump, a fixture re-blessed to a different value, `@target` silently added to a green scenario, a whole suite directory renamed away.
files.l3: The header explicitly names its own prior failure mode, per a documented review finding: two of a previous round's 48 cases didn't actually test what they claimed — one was three greps of the gate's OWN SOURCE TEXT (would have passed even with the logic it claimed to test fully inverted), and another planted a no-op stand-in for an attack rather than the specific attack a real reviewer had actually found effective. The house rule it now enforces on itself, in the header's own words: 'A TEST THAT GREPS THE GATE'S SOURCE IS NOT A TEST' — every case here runs a real command and reads a real exit code, and where the refusal should carry a specific stated reason, the case asserts that exact reason string too, so a case can't pass merely because some unrelated leg happened to fail instead. Several cases are explicitly marked NEW-CLASS — attacks invented and tested BEFORE any human reviewer had found them, in direct response to a prior round's own closing recommendation to do exactly that; the file discloses, honestly, that these found nothing, which is itself the reported outcome rather than a gap left unstated.

files.role: Supersedes the original data model with one typed-edge graph; states the project's core laws.
files.l1: Five days after the first design shipped, the project fundamentally rethought its own data model: instead of separate hand-maintained files for places, events, and narratives, EVERYTHING would become one interconnected graph made of typed "nodes" (verses, places, events...) and typed "edges" between them (this event happened AT this place, this passage CITES that one). This document is the record of that rethink and the seven numbered design laws (like "no fabricated connections" and "proof at the boundary") every later feature is still held to.
files.l2: States seven principles (P1-P7) as binding laws, not suggestions: one compiled artifact is the single source of truth (P1); every connection is a typed, either-authored-or-derived edge, never a special case (P2); source fidelity is proven ONCE at ingestion by fail-loud compile-time checks (P3); a UI surface is just a selection of edge kinds plus a renderer, never bespoke logic (P4); a new data source is always a new "adapter," never a rewrite (P5); several long-standing product rules (like verses being immutable and containers never duplicating data) carry forward as graph laws (P6); and every subsystem is consumed only through an interface it doesn't own, so a bad implementation choice can be swapped out later without surgery on its callers (P7). Also defines the node kinds (TextSpan, Container, Event, Narrative, Place, Person, Anchor, Era, Polity, CatechismItem, Source) and edge kinds (contains, attests, confesses, succession, cross-ref, and more) as a table, and lays out a multi-stage migration plan (M-A through M-D) for getting the existing app onto this new model without ever breaking the standing test suite.
files.l3: §9a ("Storage portability") and §9b ("Community addressability") are the direct ancestors of the later relational-artifact migration spec: §9a's own language — "stores are dumb verified bytes + indexes," laws never move into the backend — is quoted verbatim as a binding ruling in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-relational-artifact-design.md` §1.3. §9b's content-addressed identity principle ("every thing's id is the hash of its canonical content") is exactly what that same later spec's §3 finds three real defects in and fixes. The "Seam inventory" table (§2, P7) is a live status tracker updated in later batches, not a one-time list — it names which architectural boundaries are DONE versus still a GAP as of the batch that most recently touched this document. §4's edge table is the direct ancestor of the `relations!` macro manifest `graph-types` uses today, and this document's own footnote that a new relation needs "a record type plus compiler rule plus display rule" is cited almost verbatim as a design constraint in the later frontend/backend contract spec's frontier-generation discussion (§9 Q5 there).

files.l1: Where the graph design spec states its rules in prose, this much longer companion document works out the actual TYPES (in Haskell for the conceptual algebra, then Rust for the real implementation, then C# for the client) needed to make every one of those rules impossible to violate by accident — a date can't be stored without saying WHY it was chosen, a traversal button can't exist unless a real edge backs it, a query result can never mysteriously stop being the same order twice.
files.l2: Opens with a Haskell sketch of exploration as a genuine monadic "bind" operation (correcting an acknowledged flaw in `BibleGraph.hs`'s own earlier, simpler encoding), then works through Rust: identity and text addressing, the closed `NodeKind` enum, a full table of typed edge relations (deliberately NOT one big untyped list — each relation's own Rust type makes an illegal edge impossible to construct), a chronology system where an event's date is always a resolved PLACEMENT against a shared anchor table rather than a bare literal (so two parts of the app can never quietly disagree about when something happened), the ingestion/adapter contract, the server-side Explorable runtime trait, a client-side presentation algebra, and the C# client contract. Closes with a long, explicit checklist (§9) of specific bad states these types make literally impossible to represent, and a list of genuinely open questions (§10) rather than pretending everything was already settled.
files.l3: §4's `DatePlacement` enum (`AnchorBinding`, `ReignYear`, `SequenceAfter`, `EraOnly`) plus its `PlacementBasis` (`Textual` vs `Traditional`) is the exact mechanism `data/curated/chronology-anchors.toml` and `server/atlas-core/src/chronology.rs` implement, replacing an earlier, explicitly REJECTED "antichain" (uncertain-order-cluster) design per a quoted, verbatim owner ruling that ordering must be as granular as necessary, down to the day, with an optional justification field baked into a claim's own content-addressed identity when a date rests on adopted tradition rather than the text itself. §2's `NodeKind` enum comment states the discipline directly: extending a closed Rust enum forces the compiler to flag every match site that needs updating, so "a new node kind is a record + compiler rule + display rule — the exhaustive match IS the checklist." §9's impossibility checklist is effectively the acceptance criteria every later batch touching the graph schema is measured against, including entries added well after this document's own nominal date (e.g. corpus-erased correspondence and cross-corpus quoting, which point directly at the later `2026-08-24-corpus-correspondence-design.md`).

files.role: Proposal for linking loci across different corpora (Bible↔Concord, Hebrew↔Greek), unshipped by design.
files.l1: Once the Book of Concord became a second text corpus alongside the Bible, an obvious question followed: how should the graph represent "this passage in one corpus is really the same underlying content as that passage in a different corpus" — a Confession quoting Scripture, or (the document's own worked example) the Greek Old Testament translating a Hebrew word in a way that later shapes how the New Testament quotes it? This document proposes an answer but explicitly ships ZERO code changes — it's a proposal awaiting the project owner's own review before anyone implements it.
files.l2: Explains what already exists (three narrower relations — `Quotes`, `Confesses`, and a same-corpus-only `Corresponds<C>`) and why none of them can express a genuinely cross-corpus claim, then proposes widening `Corresponds` into a corpus-erased form carrying a `CorrespondenceClass` tag (`Translation`, `Editorial`, or `Quotation`) so it can honestly state "these two loci in DIFFERENT corpora are the same underlying material." Works the proposal through a real worked example (Isaiah 7:14's Hebrew "almah" versus the Greek Septuagint's "parthenos," versus Matthew's own citation of the Greek wording) and a nearer-term one (extracting the Book of Concord's hundreds of inline Bible citations, once this design is approved). Ends with four explicitly unresolved open questions for the owner and a stated list of non-goals for this document itself.
files.l3: The worked example in §4 is carefully framed to stay inside the project's own KJV-inerrancy discipline: it states explicitly that a Hebrew-to-Greek TRANSLATION difference is 'a fact about translation history across corpora,' never a claim that the KJV itself is wrong or uncertain — the same register already established for the six brain-fuel/bible parallel-language editions. §6 discloses the author's own personal lean between two migration options (retire the old type-parameterized `Corresponds<C>` entirely, or keep both forms) WITHOUT deciding it, an explicit example of this project's discipline of separating "what I'd recommend" from "what was ruled." §5 notes, concretely, that Bible↔Concord citation extraction, once implemented, would be MOSTLY a matter of finally populating two relations (`Quotes`, `Confesses`) that already exist in the schema today but sit permanently empty — a fact independently confirmed by `server/atlas-graph/src/artifact.rs`'s own disclosed 'SCOPE' comment. As of this document, the Corpus correspondence design remains unimplemented; no crate in `server/` or `graph-types/` yet defines the widened `Corresponds` or `CorrespondenceClass` types it proposes.

files.role: The plan to replace the single bincode graph.bin with a manifest + attached SQLite sections.
files.l1: This is the newest and most consequential design document in the repo: a plan to stop treating the compiled data as one giant file that must be fully loaded into memory at every server startup, and instead split it into several separately-named database files (one per corpus) that a query can read from without loading the whole thing — while also fixing three real, quietly-accumulated bugs in how the app computes content-addressed ids. Nothing in this document is implemented yet; it's owner-approved as a plan, not as code.
files.l2: States the core idea in one paragraph (§0): a small manifest file, committed to git, names one read-only SQLite file per corpus ('section'), each named by a hash of its own content; the server attaches these as one combined database and serves through the SAME existing query interface, now widened by six new methods. Explains what changes and what deliberately doesn't (the compiler still builds one in-memory graph and runs every validation law over it exactly as before — the database is just a different OUTPUT ENCODING of an already-proven-correct graph, never a new source of rules). §3 walks through three real defects in the current identity scheme (the version root doesn't cover edges/rows, only nodes; the hash algorithm is Rust's own unspecified, un-pinned `DefaultHasher`; there's no compiler-version pin at all) plus a fourth found while writing this spec (identity is computed from debug-print text output, which can't be decoded back into the original data). Lays out a complete, reviewed database schema (§5) and a batch-by-batch delivery order (§8) where each batch is independently valuable even if the next one never happens.
files.l3: §1.3 makes an explicit, cited ruling AGAINST an earlier proposal (from the prerequisite research plan this spec supersedes) to move some validation rules into SQL foreign keys and unique indexes — rejected specifically so the existing ~1,069-line `law_check.rs` validation module never needs to be rewritten, quoting the original graph design spec's own §9a language ('stores are dumb verified bytes + indexes... no schema constraints, no triggers') as the binding precedent. §3.4 documents a real engineering trade-off made transparently: the original brainstorm wanted BLAKE3 for hashing, but that's a crate dependency, and `graph-types` is contractually required to have none (the sibling map project path-depends on it being dependency-free) — so the spec settles on a hand-written SHA-256 implementation truncated to 128 bits instead, with the exact reasoning shown, not just the conclusion. §8's batch table (TOOLCHAIN-1 through LEX-1) is the direct blueprint for `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-14-toolchain1-contention1.md`, which implements exactly the first two rows. §13 closes out, row by row, the nine open questions from an earlier, separate research plan this document explicitly supersedes, and §14 states five falsifiable acceptance criteria (e.g. 'a new corpus is a new section and changes no other section's hash, no loader code, and no port code') any future implementation of this spec must actually satisfy, not merely claim.

files.l1: Before any part of the big database migration plan could safely begin, two smaller problems had to be fixed first: the Rust compiler version wasn't pinned anywhere (so a routine `rustup update` could silently change every content-hashed id in the whole app with zero real data change), and eight tests that measure wall-clock time were flaky simply because they sometimes ran at the same time as other slow tests and competed for the CPU. This plan fixes both, as two small, independently-shippable batches, before any actual database work starts.
files.l2: Four numbered tasks: pin the toolchain in this repo (`rust-toolchain.toml` plus a test proving the compiler that built the test binary really is the pinned version), pin the toolchain in the sibling map project the same way, mark all eight timing-sensitive tests `#[ignore]` with one exact, machine-checked reason string and add a script (`scripts/timing-gates.sh`, not itself part of this writer's assigned files) that runs each of them alone in its own process, and update the project's own documented test-counting procedure and README to describe the new three-command total. A final acceptance task requires ten consecutive full test-suite runs with zero flips before calling the batch done — a directly measured claim, not an assumed one.
files.l3: This plan is the literal, immediate execution of exactly the first two rows (TOOLCHAIN-1 and CONTENTION-1) of `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-14-relational-artifact-design.md` §8's own batch table — its own "Spec" line cites that document by section number directly. Explicitly states the ceilings it touches are NEVER to be loosened (artifact load 4s, full-graph conformance 60s, `perf_smoke`'s six named thresholds) — only WHERE those tests run changes (serialized, one process each), never the pass/fail bar itself, matching `server/BENCHMARKS.md`'s own standing discipline of never chasing a number down by weakening the test that measures it. Its own "File Structure" table names the exact ignore-reason string used verbatim everywhere (grepped byte-for-byte by its own self-test script) — a small but concrete example of this project's habit of making a convention machine-checkable rather than merely documented.
